PASSO 1: imagine uma data no futuro, por: STEP 1: picture a future date, say Friday. In English: "By Friday I will have finished the report." That "will have finished" is the futuro perfecto. STEP 2: Spanish builds it with the simple future of «haber» + participle: «habré terminado». English "will have" = «habré», in one word. STEP 3: the future of «haber»: habré, habrás, habrá, habremos, habréis, habrán. Four of them have an accent (habré, habrás, habrá, habréis); «habremos» doesn't. STEP 4: the participle is the usual one (hablado, comido, vivido; hecho, dicho, visto, puesto, escrito, abierto, vuelto…) and it NEVER agrees with the subject. STEP 5: use the futuro perfecto to say an action will be finished before a future moment. The typical markers are «para + time» — English "BY Friday" is «PARA el viernes», «para entonces» (by then) — and «antes de + time» («antes de las ocho»). Careful: "by" here is never «por». STEP 6: compare: «terminaré el informe» (I'll finish the report, some time) and «habré terminado el informe para el viernes» (by Friday it will be done). STEP 7: negation and pronouns go before the auxiliary: «No habré terminado», «Lo habré terminado» (I will have finished it). STEP 8: in everyday conversation, for concrete plans, many people prefer the present («para el viernes lo tengo listo» = I'll have it ready by Friday). The futuro perfecto for plans is more common in writing and formal situations; its most frequent use is guessing, which you'll see in the next session.

PASSO 1: o futuro não serve só para fala: STEP 1: the future isn't only for what will happen. Spanish also uses it to GUESS about right now: «Pablo estará en casa» means "Pablo is probably at home" / "Pablo must be at home". STEP 2: the same goes for questions: «¿Dónde estará Pablo?» means "I wonder where Pablo is". English needs "I wonder"; Spanish just puts the verb in the future. As an old grammar for English speakers puts it, "to wonder" is often best translated by the future of probability: "Has he come yet, I wonder?" = «¿Habrá venido ya?», "I wonder who that man is" = «¿Quién será ese hombre?». STEP 3: to guess about something that has just happened, use the futuro perfecto: «Habrá llegado ya» (he must have arrived by now), «¿Habrá perdido el autobús?» (I wonder if he missed the bus). STEP 4: notice the difference in certainty. «Ha llegado» states a fact. «Habrá llegado» is a guess — like English "he'll have arrived by now". STEP 5: the guess can be negative: «No habrá visto el mensaje» (he probably hasn't seen the message). STEP 6: an alternative is «deber de» + infinitive, like English "must": «Debe de estar en casa» (he must be at home), «Debe de haber llegado» (he must have arrived). In speech many people drop the «de» with the same meaning; be careful, because «debes hacerlo» without «de» is an obligation ("you must do it"). STEP 7: for a guess about a more distant past, Spanish uses the conditional: «Entonces tendría unos veinte años» (he must have been about twenty then). You only need to recognise it. STEP 8: words like «seguramente», «probablemente» and «supongo que» reinforce the guess.

PASSO 1: a suposição pode ter ajuda de u: STEP 1: a guess can come with a helper expression: «seguramente, probablemente, supongo que, me imagino que, seguro que». STEP 2: after «supongo que», «me imagino que» and «seguro que», use the indicative, as you already do: «Supongo que ha llegado», «Seguro que viene de camino» (I bet he's on his way). STEP 3: «a lo mejor» is very colloquial and means "maybe". It also takes the indicative: «A lo mejor ha perdido el autobús». STEP 4: «quizá» and «tal vez» also mean "maybe/perhaps", but they can take another verb form that you'll learn in lesson 43. For now, use «a lo mejor». STEP 5: when you use one of these expressions, the future is optional: «Seguramente habrá llegado» and «Seguro que ha llegado» are both natural. STEP 6: to link guesses, use «o», «y», «como»: «O no ha oído el despertador, o ha perdido el autobús» (Either… or…). STEP 7: false friend: «seguramente» means "probably", not "securely" or "for sure" — for certainty, say «seguro» or «sin duda».
